item.title: Two people convicted in relation to death of French streamer
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c8rnmdy4enpo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Two people convicted in relation to death of French streamer - Published Two people in France have been convicted of aggravated violence, following an investigation into the death of a French streamer known for extreme challenges. Raphaël Graven, 46, died in a village near Nice in August 2025. His death was live broadcast on the streaming platform Kick. The internet personality was routinely subjected to humiliation and abuse in his content, which the convicted men, Safine Hamadi and Owen Cenazandotti, said occurred with his consent. Hamadi and Cenazandotti have each been issued suspended prison sentences for their role in Graven's death, and ordered to pay fines of €5,000 (£4283) and €15,000 (£12,848) respectively. Neither man was charged with the manslaughter of Graven, also known as Jean Pormanove, after the prosecution said probable causes of death appeared to be related to his poor health and fragile heart. The court also acquitted them of abusing Graven's psychological frailty, as he had told police prior to his death that he had consented to the stunts, Hamadi's lawyer told Reuters. Hamadi, who expressed remorse during the trial, received an 18-month suspended prison sentence. Cenazandotti received a two-year suspended prison sentence. Both men have been banned from posting on Kick for six months. Kick, the streaming platform, remains under investigation by French authorities. In a statement to the New York Times on Thursday, it said it was not a party to the proceedings against Hamadi and Cenazandotti, and had no comment on the outcome. It added: "The ruling relates solely to two individual content creators." Graven had more than one million followers across his various social media platforms and had built a strong community on Kick. During broadcasts on the platform, other streamers would regularly subject the 46-year-old to acts of violence and verbal humiliation. Graven was found dead in Contes, a village north of Nice, in August 2025. Local media at the time reported that a livestream on 18 August showed the man lying lifeless on a mattress covered with a duvet. The video has since been removed from Kick. item.title: Israel charges settler over killing of Palestinian involved in Oscar-winning West Bank film
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cn4n1e8159yo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Israel charges settler over killing of Palestinian involved in Oscar-winning West Bank film - Published Israeli prosecutors have charged a settler over the killing of a Palestinian activist in the occupied West Bank who helped film Oscar-winning documentary No Other Land. Yinon Levy was charged with reckless manslaughter over the July 2025 shooting of Odeh Hathaleen, according to Israel's Southern District Prosecutor's Office. Israeli rights group B'Tselem said it was the first time an Israeli had been indicted for killing a Palestinian in the West Bank for nearly three years. A lawyer for Hathaleen's family said they hoped the charges marked a "turning point" in the consequences settlers face for violence against Palestinians. In a letter seen by The Associated Press, Levy said he would fight for his innocence in court. He wrote that prosecutors should not penalise acts of self-defence and accused them of providing "de facto support for terrorism", the news agency reported. A lawyer for Levy, Avichai Hajbi, told the AP the prosecution had made a "mistaken decision". The charges against Levy also include armed trespassing and malicious property damage during the incident in which settlers operated an excavator in the Palestinian village of Umm al-Khair, leading to a confrontation with residents. According to the indictment, at some point during the confrontation Levy cocked his gun and fired in the direction of residents, hitting Hathaleen. He then fired another shot into the air, prosecutors said. Footage of the incident was shared widely online. Levy has previously denied firing the shot that killed Hathaleen. The indictment is the first since the 7 October 2023 Hamas-led attack on southern Israel which triggered the Gaza war and led to a rise in settler violence in the West Bank, B'Tselem said. At least 1,110 Palestinians have been killed by Israeli soldiers and settlers in the West Bank since then, according to the UN. At least 41 Israelis have been killed either by a Palestinian armed group or civilian in the West Bank during the same period, the UN said. B'Tselem described the decision to indict Levy as the "exception that proves the rule". "The impunity Israel grants to soldiers and settlers who harm Palestinians is not a failure of the system - it is a central component of a policy designed to allow the violence to continue and escalate," it said. Mattan Berner-Kadish, an Israeli-American activist who was at the scene, told the BBC: "I think the general reaction is happiness that anything is happening while also feeling that it should be a murder charge and a longer maximum sentence. "Mixed feelings but also certainly pleasantly surprised and happy there might be consequences," he added. Hathaleen, a teacher and father-of-three, was a prominent voice against settler violence in the occupied West Bank. He featured in the 2025 Oscar-winning film No Other Land, that follows the legal fight between the Israeli government and Palestinians over Masafer Yatta, a West Bank community of about 20 villages. Israel's Supreme Court ruled to allow the demolition of homes and expulsion of more than 1,000 villagers in 2022. Levy, a leader of an outpost farm, was sanctioned by the UK in 2024 because he "used physical aggression, threatened families at gunpoint, and destroyed property as part of a targeted and calculated effort to displace Palestinian communities", the UK government said at the time. He denied the allegations to the BBC in 2024. He was also sanctioned by the US under the Biden administration but those sanctions were subsequently lifted under President Donald Trump. Additional reporting by Mallory Moench - Published26 July

item.title: Doge overstated claims to have saved Americans $110bn, watchdog finds
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cvg0rg9wmvlo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Doge overstated claims to have saved Americans $110bn, watchdog finds - Published Some estimates made by Doge, the body charged with reducing US government spending, that it saved billions of dollars are "incorrect or lack supporting evidence", a watchdog has found. A report released on Thursday by the Government Accountability Office (GAO) has given an extensive review of Doge's claims about its so-called "Wall of Receipts", which reported savings of $110bn (£82bn) across contracts, grants and leases. "Several issues limit the transparency and reliability of these reported savings," the report stated. Asked for comment, a White House official said the administration told the GAO that all employees had to complete ethics training and follow financial disclosure requirements. Doge, the Department of Government Efficiency, was not an official government department. It launched at the start of President Trump's second term but closed last month. Its Wall of Receipts was a way of showing its purported savings in taxpayer money online. Elon Musk, the billionaire boss of Tesla and SpaceX who formerly led Doge but left in May 2025, initially promised to save as much as $2tn a year by slashing federal jobs and shuttering government programmes, among other cost-cutting measures. Even by Doge's own estimates, it fell short of that goal, as its website claims to have saved an estimated $214bn. "While Doge provided some information about estimated savings, several issues limit the transparency and reliability of these reported savings," the GAO report stated. It said Doge had not been transparent regarding the methods it used to calculate savings, highlighting it "did not provide sufficient information to verify the method used to calculate 96% of Doge-reported savings". Among its specific findings was that 108 of the 264 leases identified by Doge for termination were already in the process of ending before the body was established. That accounts for about $15.3m of the total $53.5m in savings Doge claimed. "The Wall of Receipts does not include an explanation of how the savings from terminated leases were calculated," the GAO said. Claims were also made about savings that were not achieved, like $1.7bn for ending a defence department contract for IT services. However, the contract was never terminated and thus no savings were achieved, according to the congressional watchdog's report. "While the Wall of Receipts includes some information about the data and sources underlying reported savings, it does not sufficiently disclose limitations affecting data quality," it assessed. The GAO audit, which was carried out at the request of Democratic Senators Gary Peters and Richard Blumenthal, covered savings data reported from 20 January 2025 through 7 July 2026. "Everyone supports rooting out waste, fraud, and abuse in the federal government, but Doge was a slapdash and deceptive effort that misled the American people while doing real damage to the government's ability to serve them," Senator Peters said in a statement on Thursday. Under Musk, Doge pushed for massive reductions in the federal workforce, as well as the shuttering of programmes and even agencies such as the US Agency for International Development (USAID). Some of Doge's moves were met with legal fights, or were reversed. When the group's cost-cutting resulted in bird flu officials at the US Department of Agriculture being fired, the Trump administration looked to re-hire them days later. In a social media post last month announcing its closure, Doge said: "While the formal mission of Doge has come to an end, the mission to eliminate waste, fraud, and abuse will continue. Good stewardship of taxpayer dollars and accountable government are not temporary initiatives." Related topics - Published30 May 2025 - Published10 December 2025

item.title: The phone book that led us to Assad's spy chief in hiding
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c4gyrzn8p94o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
The phone book that led us to Assad's spy chief in hiding - Published In an abandoned luxury apartment in the Syrian capital Damascus, armed men dressed in military fatigues sifted through designer clothes and documents. Scattered across the living room floor, under a sparkling crystal chandelier, were dozens of photos of the same slender man in different settings - sitting at his desk, even playing in the snow. And multiple prints of the same image, showing him smiling warmly as he shook the hand of ousted dictator Bashar al-Assad. The man was not instantly recognisable, but gold medals and gilded certificates piled nearby were inscribed with the name Hussam Luka. Known as "The Spider", Luka was one of Assad's top henchmen, accused of orchestrating atrocities and systematic torture, and sanctioned by the UK, US and European Union. As head of Syria's most powerful civilian intelligence agency, Luka was among the most feared men in the country. But much of his work was conducted from the shadows. Like others in the regime, Luka seemingly vanished overnight in December 2024 when Assad was toppled, leaving a trail of unanswered questions and demands for justice that many fear will never be realised. In his apartment, days after Assad's fall, we watched the rebels looking for clues as to where he might have gone. In the corner of the living room, on a console table, was an unremarkable-looking notebook. Inside, in scribbled blue handwriting, we found dozens of names - from shopkeepers and doctors, to military officials and people with the Luka family name. Could these contacts help us learn more about The Spider and his crimes, or even help us to track him down? At one time, Luka's own phone number was hard to avoid - in the early days of the Syrian civil war, it had been spray-painted on walls around the central city of Homs. The conflict was sparked by Assad's brutal crushing of a pro-democracy uprising in 2011 - a war in which hundreds of thousands of people would go on to be killed. Luka was a local head of the Political Security Directorate, one of Assad's main intelligence agencies, and had been given the task of wresting the city from the rebels. At the time, rebel-held areas in Homs were under siege by the government, and residents were struggling to access food and medicine. Several people, including former rebel fighter Motaz al-Zaydi, told us they had resorted to eating rats. Al-Zaydi remembers Luka's name and phone number appearing on a wall in his neighbourhood, and said the message began to spread that those wanting to flee the fighting could phone the number for safe passage. Some are believed to have been granted safe transit out of the city by Luka, but others who called the number were never seen or heard from again, according to several people we spoke to, including al-Zaydi. Many told us they referred to Luka as "The Spider" because of his vast web of allies and informants, including some embedded in rebel groups. "He was everywhere," Homs residents told us. Al-Zaydi described Luka as an "evil genius" and "a fox of a man". But his most egregious action in the city, many argue, was his alleged involvement in the so-called Eid Massacre, known by some as the Children's Massacre, which the US noted when sanctioning him. It was the Muslim holiday of Eid al-Adha in September 2015, and Mohammed Towakatli's seven-year-old, Wael, was gardening in the playground he had set up in the al-Waer neighbourhood. At 17:10, just after the power ration had kicked in, Mohammed remembers the strike hitting. As Mohammed walked around the park earlier this year, now planted with rows of saplings, he recalled the names of the children killed and the games they had been playing at the time, gesturing to the places where he had found their bodies, including that of Wael. "They were tiny children," he said with tears in his eyes. "The ground here was painted red with blood." Twenty-eight people were killed, including 17 children and four women, according to the Syrian Network for Human Rights. Luka, according to a Syrian activist group, and a pro-opposition newspaper at the time, was responsible for the regime's selection of targets in the area that day. His actions in Homs earned him a promotion, and by the time of the regime's collapse he ran the General Security Directorate (GSD) intelligence agency, making him one of the most powerful people in the country. The government security services could target anyone - from opposition fighters, journalists, doctors, or rights activists, to people believed to be opposed in any form to the Assad government. Those arrested were detained in Syria's political prisons, including Sednaya in Damascus - a facility so notorious it was dubbed the "human slaughterhouse". Many imprisoned there were never seen again. As head of the GSD, Luka had strategic control over Syria's detention policies, and his personnel would monitor communications to and from Sednaya. There are widespread calls across Syrian society on social media for former senior officials to be held accountable. Some also say the new Syrian government is not doing enough to bring these people to justice. Syria's Attorney General, Hassan al-Turba, told the BBC the government had launched a lawsuit against Luka, accusing him of "premeditated murder, torture, and death resulting from torture". "A warrant has been circulated domestically and we are working on circulating it internationally as well," he said, adding the administration was working to track the location and seek the extradition of Luka and other missing senior regime officials. As he continues to grieve for his son, Mohammed told the BBC he wanted Luka, alongside other senior regime officials, to be returned to Syria and executed. "They look like humans but have no humanity in them at all," he said. We had taken photos of every page of the book we discovered in Luka's apartment and, back in London, began testing every one of its 155 numbers - aware that many people close to the regime would have fled or gone to ground. Fifty-one numbers appeared to be operational. We then called these again in order of their apparent importance to Luka, starting with military commanders and relatives. Every call was unsuccessful. Anyone who answered simply hung up when we explained who we were and what we wanted - or denied knowing Luka or his family, or even being the people listed in the book. So a BBC reporter, whose own name was once on a GSD wanted list while Luka ran the agency, headed to Syria to try in person. Many of those listed in the phone book were doctors, so our reporter began booking medical appointments with some of them as a way to meet them. A doctor in Aleppo reluctantly acknowledged he had treated Luka, but then ordered our journalist to leave and returned his consultation fee. Our reporter then booked an appointment with another doctor in the phone book, this time based in Damascus. This doctor revealed he had once accompanied Luka's mother on a medical trip to Russia, but was reluctant to give us any more information, other than to vaguely direct us to a pharmacy belonging to one of Luka's daughters. Locals said she, too, had not been seen since December 2024. For months we drew a blank in our hunt for Luka. And then we had our first breakthrough. One of those listed in the book, who we tried calling again, finally answered the phone. He had been the guard for Luka's apartment block, he told us, and eventually agreed to give us the number for someone he said had been Luka's personal bodyguard - a man we are calling Mahmoud. It took weeks to secure an interview with Mahmoud. Meetings would be scheduled but he would not show up, or he would request a meeting in a private space such as a car or apartment, which our reporter judged too much of a risk. They eventually met at a hotel one night, just before midnight. Broad-shouldered and physically imposing, Mahmoud seemed to be considering every answer carefully before he spoke. He told us he was angry with Luka for leaving him behind when the regime fell. As word had spread in December 2024 that Assad's rule was on the brink of collapse - with rebels advancing on the capital - Luka had said he would stay and defend Damascus, Mahmoud told us. But by the early hours of the next morning, Luka had disappeared, taking a large sum of money with him from the office safe, Mahmoud said. Mahmoud refused to share any contact details for Luka or his family, but did give us a number for Luka's driver, who he believed had driven the former spy chief out of the capital that night. This man proved even harder to reach. When he answered the phone, his voice was nervous and unsteady. He repeatedly insisted he was just a driver, and knew nothing of Luka's activities. Multiple meetings with us were never kept, and eventually he stopped replying. We turned our attention to Luka's possible escape routes, including neighbouring Lebanon - where the Iran-backed group Hezbollah had close links with the Assad regime. One senior source in the Lebanese government told us he understood Luka had passed through Lebanon on a "good Russian passport but with a different name", before flying out to Russia. We managed to find a man, now based in Lebanon, whose name was listed in Luka's contacts book, but under a number that no longer worked. He is one of many wanted by the new Syrian government, because of his close association with the Assad regime. This man, who we cannot identify, said he had a number for Luka. We saw it, and realised it had a Russian country code. Russia was a key backer of the Assad regime, and in the days after his fall, Assad released a statement confirming that he had fled there. Many of his inner circle were believed to have followed him. Back in Luka's apartment in Damascus, we had found clues that Luka also had strong links to Moscow - awards from Russia's foreign spy service, and even a New Year's card addressed to him from a senior Russian official. Now, the Russian telephone number for him suggested we finally had proof that he was - as we had predicted - in Russia. We wanted to verify that this number really was Luka's. So a few days later, with us present, the man agreed to put the person he said was Hussam Luka on speakerphone, and ask him questions which we believed only Luka would know the answer to, based on information we had gathered during our investigation. The voice on the other end of the phone sounded confused, but answered the questions instantly and correctly. He refused, however, to speak to us directly. But our contact later agreed to call Luka again and allow us to try to interview him. The same voice answered, and we introduced ourselves, explaining that we had questions about serious allegations relating to massacres and torture committed by the former regime official. "I can't take any risk talking on the phone in the position I'm in," Luka said, his tone anxious. Asked if Russia was blocking him from talking, Luka said: "I cannot talk. I can't explain. You have to understand." When asked if he would meet us outside Russia, he said: "It's difficult." He then hung up the phone. We later obtained a second number which we were told was also for Luka - this time registered in Syria and linked to social media and messaging apps which he appeared to be still using. Over a period of a day, the BBC was able to locate him in two suburban areas on the outskirts of the Russian capital, Moscow. The locations seemed far removed from the luxurious lifestyle Assad is reported to be leading in exile in Russia, and to the life Luka himself once led in Syria. We knew we could not approach him in person in Russia, where Assad's henchmen are shielded from international journalists and police, so we decided to try putting our allegations to him over the phone once again. We rang the number and the same voice as before answered, the line crackly. He asked who was calling, and when told it was the BBC, he immediately hung up. We sent a message over WhatsApp, asking for his response to the many allegations against him, but he did not reply. Confirmation that Luka is in Moscow is difficult news for those in Syria seeking justice. Russia is highly unlikely to extradite officials from the regime that it long supported. The Russian government did not respond to BBC requests for comment about Luka's presence there, or whether it would ever consider an extradition request. Back in Homs, Mohammed says he will never let go of the hope that Luka, and other senior members of the Assad regime, will one day face justice. "[I am] angry at all those who were with the regime and its security apparatus… They were all against us," he says. "Wael was just a seven-year-old child… All he cared about was playing and having fun." Additional reporting by Riam Dalati, Ghaith Solh and Abigail Akerman

========================================
He's been frozen on Everest for 30 years, now 'Green Boots' may finally be coming home - Published For 30 years, a dead body known as "Green Boots" has been lying in the snow, nestled under an overhanging rock, not far from Mount Everest's summit. The lime mountaineering boots worn by an Indian climber who died in 1996 have been a grim trail marker for many climbers on their way up the world's highest peak ever since. Now India is looking for a specialist high-altitude recovery team to undertake a complex and risky mission to retrieve what they say is Dorje Morup's body – arguably the most famous of the hundreds whose bodies have been left frozen on the mountain. They hope they are on the cusp of returning his remains to friends and family who never gave up hope he'd come home. "On some days, before I went to sleep, I would think that there'd be a knock on the door tonight and that when I opened, he would be there," Morup's wife told the BBC. "When he comes home, I will ask him: 'Where were you all these years?'" Disaster struck on descent The night before he left to be part of a historic Indian expedition on Everest, Morup sat with his wife at his home in Ladakh, an Indian-administered territory in another part of the Himalayas. He made her a promise: that he would come back a hero and make his country proud. "He asked me to take care of the kids and come to the airport to greet him on his return," Konchak Yangskit told the BBC at her home. A lance naik, or lance corporal, in the Indo Tibetan Border Police (ITBP), the force guarding much of India's border with China, 48-year-old Morup was no stranger to Himalayan trekking. But Yangskit says she had a strange sense of foreboding that night: "I wondered if I was ever going to see him again." Morup was one of six climbers on the ITBP expedition attempting to reach the top of Everest – which lies on the border between Nepal and the Chinese-governed territory of Tibet. Most climbers choose to ascend from the Nepalese side, but Morup's crew wanted to write their names into the history books as the first Indian expedition to do it from the treacherous Chinese side. Three out of six members of the expedition turned back due to a snowstorm, but Morup and two others - Tsewang Smanla and Tsewang Paljor – kept struggling, all the way up to the 8,849m summit. Disaster, a blizzard, struck as they descended and killed all three. Like many of the more than 300 people who have died in the Everest region since records began a century ago, their bodies remain on the mountain. Two have never been found, but the third body - that of "Green Boots" - has been lying frozen in the snow for three decades at an altitude of 8,500 metres. For years, it was assumed that "Green Boots" was another member of the expedition, Tsewang Paljor. But testimony from surviving members of the 1996 expedition and the location of the last radio contact with the climbers have now led authorities to believe the remains belong to Morup. An ITBP official, speaking anonymously because he is not authorised to speak to the media, told BBC News Hindi that Morup's clothes and climbing gear helped officials identify the body in recent years. Since then, they've been plotting how to get their comrade home so they can confirm his identity beyond doubt through DNA testing and offer his family a semblance of closure. "We never forgot him. It was only a matter of time," the ITBP official said. How difficult will it be to recover the body? Retrieving those who have died on the mountain is a dangerous, gruelling task, and, up until the past decade, very rare. Many of the bodies, like Morup's, are in what climbers call Everest's death zone – where temperatures can plunge to -40C and oxygen levels are about a third of those at sea level. "The weather and snow conditions are going to be crucial," said Tshiring Jangbu Sherpa, a prominent Nepalese mountaineer who has taken part in other recovery missions. "The north side has fewer crevasses, but it is riskier. If something bad happens from the Nepalese side, you get quickly evacuated by helicopter. But there is no such system from the Chinese side," he told BBC Hindi. The Chinese side of the peak – where Green Boots' body is – is steeper and doesn't have the same support structures as the southern slope, which is another complicating factor, Sherpa sources have told BBC News Nepali. "It's really tough to get that body down even in popular spring season, let alone the autumn [which has more unpredictable weather]. That's the simple reason it is still there for so many years," mountaineering guide Pemba Ongchu Sherpa said. "There would need to be 10 to 12 climbers who are capable of making summits, just to fix [support] ropes to reach that point." Green Boots will also have to be physically carried down to an altitude where it can be collected by a helicopter, or possibly yaks, and transported back to an airport – a job which also requires huge manpower. Sherpas say bodies shrouded in iced-up climbing gear often weigh several times the average man and are frequently frozen into awkward positions, making bringing them down the challenging terrain even more treacherous. The remains may also begin defrosting and decomposing once they reach lower altitudes. The start of the descent with the body would be the most difficult, Indian climber Kuntal Joisher told BBC Nepali. "It's going to be very, very risky endeavour. It's extremely steep ground with lots of rock. Logistically, this [first] 1000m is going to be a humungous challenge." "The main thing is to not put Sherpa lives at risk for a dead body." All of this makes for a hugely expensive recovery mission – experts say even the most straightforward ones cost between $40,000 and $80,000, a sum beyond the means of most families. It is more common for local teams to move people who have died out of view on the mountain: like explorer Francys Arsentiev, dubbed the Sleeping Beauty of Everest, who in 2007 was moved to a more private final resting place on Everest almost a decade after she died. But the ITBP – which is funding the recovery operation – wants Morup's body to be returned by September, and is looking for mountain rescue Sherpa groups who could do the job. Once returned to India, the body will undergo DNA testing and, if confirmed to be Morup, his remains will be given back to his family. 'My heart refused to believe he had died' For years, Morup's family back in Ladakh have struggled to come to terms with his disappearance. Now around 75, Yangskit struggles to recall even the day she was married. But the days after the tragedy remain etched in her mind. "I only knew there was a storm on the mountain. Even though we organised cremation prayers at home, my heart refused to believe he had died," she says with tears rolling down her face. "I didn't see his dead body, so it was difficult for me to believe it." All that remains of Morup today are his medals and trophies, a couple of old photos from his mountain adventures – and, most importantly, a certificate from the Chinese government which states that at 17:30 on 10 May 1996, Morup reached the top of Everest. If the recovery mission is successful, Morup's son Punchok Dorjai told the BBC that the family would hold a funeral for him near the Martyrs Park in Ladakh's capital Leh. "My father gave his life for the country and he should be remembered as a martyr," Dorjai said, adding that his teammates who perished deserve the same title. The family will also proudly save a symbol of Morup's legacy at their home, to go alongside his summit certification, he said: "We are planning to keep the Green Boots." Additional reporting by Pradeep Bashyal, BBC News Nepali

item.title: Scale of devastation shocks US city's fire-seasoned residents
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cvglpvgljzdo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Scale of devastation shocks US city's fire-seasoned residents - Published Last year, Chris Matthews was forced to flee with his family of five after a brushfire threatened their home in Spokane, Washington. That evacuation lasted only a few hours. So when an ominous column of dark smoke raced towards him last Saturday, and he and his family were evacuated again, he expected he'd be back home soon. Instead, he returned to find nothing but smouldering ruins. "All of us thought we were going to be able to get back to our houses," he recalls. "And we didn't think it'd be a situation where we were going to lose our homes or anything like that." Smoke and fires are a normal occurrence here in the US Pacific Northwest every summer, as residents wait for the autumn rains to arrive. Small evacuations are not unexpected. But the scale of this year's fires in Spokane is unprecedented. Kira Townsend, 39, says she realised the immense danger when word came that the fire had jumped over the river, which normally acts as a barrier protecting the city from fires. "It's never jumped the river like that, and just roared up the hill that fast," she says. Nearly a quarter of the city population – 65,000 people – were forced to evacuate since the fires began. For those whose homes did not burn down, officials say it may be weeks before it is safe to return to their neighbourhoods. Miraculously, there have been no deaths or major injuries reported from the fires. Matthew Kincanon, 31, fled for his life as the fire entered his neighbourhood of Prosperity Lane on Saturday night. He returned 12 hours later to discover that there was nothing left. "As soon as I stepped out of the car I threw up," he says. "I felt sick. I couldn't control it. I just lost it. It hit me all at once," he says. While firefighters battle three large fires around the city that remain less than 40% contained, the recovery effort is beginning for people who have lost everything. "We have two fronts going at the same time. We're actively fighting the fire and trying to put that out. But we're also starting recovering for folks that have lost their homes," City Councilman Zack Zappone, who grew up in the devastated Indian Trails neighbourhood, tells the BBC. "There just a lot of uncertainty and frustrations and difficultness," he says at a city shelter, describing the tensions in the city. Chrissy Goodrich's voice cracks in anger as she calls on people to do everything they can to prevent more wildfires. She echoes warnings from officials, who say that innocent activities like mowing your lawn could ignite a fire. "People have got to use their brains," she says. "Stop doing things that are gonna cause sparks. I can't believe someone was mowing." "So many people have lost their houses, and people are just being so stupid," she adds. She and her 73-year-old father, Scott Hansen still ride their mountain bikes through burned-out neighbourhoods to get groceries back to home, which is in the mandatory evacuation zone. Like many Spokane residents, he expressed surprise at how easily the fire breached the river. "The winds were too strong," he says. "It just blew over the river like it wasn't even there." Anger has intensified since police charged a local man, who has allegedly confessed to sparking one of the fires. "I was so happy they got him. It's just not right," says lifelong resident Susan Crouch, 70, who previously lost her home to wildfire. The fires this summer, she adds, "are the worst Spokane has ever had". Local media reported that he had previously been questioned for arson, and had a prior conviction for killing his own father in Arizona in 2010. The suspect, Aaron Farinacci, 37, has not yet entered a plea, and a judge has ordered him to undergo a mental competency evaluation. According to investigators, he specifically chose a dry, windy day, in the hopes of sparking a large fire. More dry windy days are in the forecast. Matthews, who lost his house, is now urging his neighbours to prepare for the worst. In retrospect, he says he wishes he had a generator that he could have used to power a sprinkler system around the property after the electricity went out. "For future reference, and for everyone else – take it seriously. Don't assume past historical times are what's going to happen in the future as well." His wife, Melissa Matthews, says she feels a sense of "closure" to discover that the blaze that destroyed her home may have been set intentionally by a man who is now accused of arson. "It brought a little bit of closure," she says, adding: "That sounds weird to say." Chris adds: "Knowing that a person did this, as opposed to it being a natural thing that happened, it just does feel a little bit comforting for some reason." Related topics - Published1 day ago

item.title: What is birthright citizenship and how common is birth tourism in the US?
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cn9nz5qwl8jo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
What is birthright citizenship and how common is birth tourism in the US? - Published US President Donald Trump has announced new executive orders aimed at ending so-called birth tourism in the US and limiting birthright citizenship for certain groups. It is part of a renewed effort by his administration to restrict access to US citizenship after the Supreme Court shot down Trump's first attempt in June. Birthright citizenship refers to the practice of granting citizenship to those born on US soil, with some exceptions, while birth tourism is when foreign nationals come to the US specifically to give birth and get their child citizenship. Here's what you need to know. What are Trump's latest executive orders? Trump signed two executive orders, a written order issued by a president to the federal government which does not require congressional approval, on Thursday. One expands the existing definitions of non-citizens whose children are not eligible for birthright citizenship. It prevents the automatic citizenship of babies born in the US to two non-citizen parents if one of the parents is a member of a foreign terrorist group, is a foreign government employee, has attempted to gain citizenship through fraudulent means, or is living in US territories where citizenship is not granted by US federal law. A few of those categories were already excluded under current birthright citizenship rules, but the one relating to membership of a foreign terrorist group could raise issues, according to Colleen Putzel-Kavanaugh, an associate policy analyst at the Migration Policy Institute, an independent nonpartisan research group. She said it is difficult to know how, when, and by whom membership would be determined, and it is also not clear "if the onus for proof falls on the government (to prove they are a member) or the individual (to prove they are not)". The second order, meanwhile, seeks to end the practice of birth tourism by directing the departments of state and homeland security to enhance regulations and expand enforcement against the practice. It is already illegal to travel to the US for the purpose of giving birth. According to the executive order, operators in the birth tourism industry use deceptive advertising to entice foreign nationals to give birth in the US. "They promise citizenship; access to public benefits; and short-term stays in specialised facilities, hotels, or rentals, but often fail to deliver on these promises," the order says. How does birthright citizenship work? The principle of birthright citizenship, known in legal terms as "jus soli" or "right of the soil", is enshrined in the 14th Amendment of the US Constitution. The law was originally meant to grant citizenship to American-born, formerly enslaved people following the American Civil War. Currently, nearly everyone born in the US, regardless of their parents' citizenship status, is granted US citizenship - with a few exceptions. These include children born in the US to foreign diplomats, those born to enemy soldiers during a hostile occupation of US territory, and those born in unincorporated US territories where a federal statute has not granted the right to citizenship. People born in the US territories of Puerto Rico, Guam, and the US Virgin Islands, for example, get automatic citizenship, while those born in unincorporated American Samoa are not and are instead considered "non-citizen nationals". How many birth tourists are there in the US? Trump said on Thursday that "hundreds of thousands" of babies have been born through birth tourism in the US, without providing evidence or clarifying if that figure is annual or not. There are no government figures specifically on women coming to the US on tourism visas to give birth, but there is data on foreign residents giving birth in the country. These show that just over 9,500 babies were born to foreign women in the US in 2024, according to the most recent estimate, external from the Centers for Disease Control (CDC). This is based on births registered to mothers with foreign addresses. In comparison, there were 3.7 million US births in total that same year, CDC figures show,, external meaning babies born to foreign US residents amounted to roughly 0.25% of these. However, the MPI says the government figures are likely an undercount and that foreigners could use a US address that is not their permanent home to register a birth. The MPI estimates, external that between 20,000 to 26,000 babies were born in the US annually as a result of birth tourism, which is about 0.5 to 0.7% of total annual births. This figure is based on a wider review of US census data, although their study notes that it is hard to know exact numbers for certain. "Birth tourism inherently relies on the intent of an individual to come to the US to give birth and capturing that intent in data is difficult," said Putzel-Kavanaugh. "For some women, they may be travelling and a medical emergency could necessitate birth in the US even if their intent was to give birth back in their home country." What happened at the Supreme Court? The Trump administration's argument against birthright citizenship when the case was before the Supreme Court in April relied heavily on the need to end birth tourism. Solicitor General D John Sauer argued that granting everyone born on US soil citizenship has allowed the birth tourism industry to thrive and created a "whole generation of American citizens abroad with no meaningful ties to the United States". At one point, Chief Justice John Roberts asked Sauer whether he agreed that birth tourism "has no impact on the legal analysis before us". Sauer responded that the existence of birth tourism proves that the 14th amendment has unintended consequences that would never have been approved by its creators. We live in a world now, Sauer said, "where eight billion people are one plane ride away from having a child who's a US citizen". Roberts, and ultimately the high court's majority, rejected that interpretation, saying: "Well, it's a new world. It's the same Constitution." Do other countries have birthright citizenship? Trump has repeatedly said the US is one of the only major countries that grants birthright citizenship. In fact, more than 30 countries practise automatic "jus soli" and without restriction in almost all cases. They include Brazil, Argentina and Mexico, as well as most other countries in Central and South America. The US and Canada are the only two countries considered "developed" nations by the International Monetary Fund that grant mostly unrestricted birthright citizenship. Other countries, like the UK and Australia, allow for a modified version where citizenship is automatically granted if one parent is a citizen or permanent resident.

item.title: German airport drone-bomb: Could Russia be involved?
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckgdmrxxkdxo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
German airport drone-bomb: Could Russia be involved? - Published As Germany investigates how a drone loaded with explosives reached a runway at Leipzig airport, there is renewed talk in Europe of hybrid war. The interior minister is warning of a "new level of danger" from an attack that "may involve foreign powers". There is no proof at this stage to link the flying bomb directly to Russia, which denies any role. But as well as the means and the motive, Moscow does have form. The BBC has seen details of the investigation into a plot in 2024 in which Russian-linked proxies in Poland and Lithuania not only handled drones and explosives but also delivered them to Germany. The flying bomb The quadcopter was discovered at Leipzig airport late on Tuesday night, forcing one runway into lockdown as a bomb disposal robot rolled into action. On the tarmac close by were several Ukrainian Antonov cargo planes, stripes along their enormous bodies in the blue and yellow of the country's flag. One reads, "Be Brave Like Kherson", the southern city now on the frontline of Russia's invasion. Pictures published by German media suggest the drone was a relatively small device which airport staff spotted "floating" between the Ukrainian planes. Around the same time, a DHL cargo plane collided with an "unidentified object" as it pulled up into the sky, unable to land in Leipzig. Teams are still working to establish whether that was a second drone. They are also trying to trace who launched the devices and why. A previous plot A previous Russian-backed plot involving Leipzig airport could provide clues. In 2024, a parcel containing a sophisticated incendiary device caught fire at the airport's DHL hub shortly before it was loaded onto a plane. Similar packages then ignited in the UK and Poland, causing extensive damage. A group of men are currently on trial in both Lithuania and Poland, where prosecutors believe they were part of a substantial network of proxies recruited by Russian military intelligence. But there was a subplot that has been little discussed before. Last September, Lithuanian prosecutors said that investigators had also seized RDX explosives meant for "other terrorist attacks". The amount was significant: equivalent to 6kg of TNT. "Some of the devices were manufactured to intensify the blast," the prosecutor added. The BBC has since had access to case documents that describe how several of the men on trial were paid to transport those explosives around Europe, concealed in cans of sweetcorn and chopped tomatoes. The detonators were hidden inside headphone sets. The suspects also handled drone parts and the case talks specifically of attachments, suitable for holding a bomb. Prosecutors allege that some of the items were brought into the EU from the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad. Almost two dozen suspects have been charged with terror offences, but with the men's handlers still at large, believed to be in Russia, it is not clear whether the entire network was disbanded or all the hidden material found. While there is no evidence of a link to the Leipzig drone bomb, the 2024 plot certainly highlights the potential. Vladyslav's story One of the suspects charged in Poland, a Ukrainian called Vladyslav D., described in detail to investigators how he made multiple long car trips in July 2024 following instructions from someone he knew as "Warrior". He has since pleaded not guilty in court. One message sent him to the edge of a Lithuanian forest where he found a carrier bag containing "three or four packs of headphones", soggy with rain. He had already collected two cans of corn "lightly covered with soil" from another location, telling investigators he had no idea what was inside. He was ordered to leave the headphones many hours' drive away in Poland where he noticed "a guy on a bicycle" collect them from beside the road. For another assignment he received a pin for a location inside a Lithuanian cemetery and was told to dig beneath some plastic flowers. He quickly uncovered a bin bag wrapped in brown tape. "Inside were drone components: small plastic propellers, I think four pieces," Vladyslav told investigators. These items were to be left by a road in central Poland for pick-up. Finally there was a trip to Germany where he was given the code to access a hostel room in Dusseldorf. He was instructed to leave the drones and other items inside. The intended targets were never revealed. Moscow's motive? In statements to investigators, Vladyslav D. said he was paid more than $2,000 (£1,487) in cryptocurrency for his efforts. His motive was clear. And what about the Leipzig case? Few details about the drone bomb are yet public. Some German sources report that the explosive was Semtex, which contains RDX - the explosive found in the food cans in a Lithuanian cemetery. We do not know how much the drone found at the airport was carrying and the physical damage may have been limited. "The drone casing, if it was metal, might have put a hole in the plane but just a blast wave probably would just have dented it unless they put some fragmentation inside," explosives expert Professor Jackie Akhavan of Cranfield University explained. But if Russia was behind this, its aim was more likely to sow fear. Andrei Soldatov, an expert on Russia's intelligence agencies, said it "makes sense" to suspect Moscow, pointing to a clear pattern of sabotage and hostile activity, from arson attacks on facilities supporting Ukraine to drones over sensitive sites in Europe. Germany is one of Kyiv's biggest suppliers of military aid. "It's a message. You get something like that [bomb] into one of the biggest European airports and you send the message that, 'Guys, we can do that. Remember'," Soldatov explained. "You hint to the adversary that you might cause a really big problem: that tomorrow might be more serious." And the potential motive? Moscow is under intense pressure from Ukraine's long-scale drone attacks, he said, and the fact that Russian President Vladimir Putin "has been humiliated, repeatedly". International response "We are aware of the incident, which the German authorities continue to investigate," a Nato official told the BBC. Antonov Airlines has also been cautious so far in its response. The firm supplies planes for certain Nato operations but declined to say whether that includes military support for Ukraine. Asked whether the Ukrainian planes might have been targeted, a spokeswoman in Kyiv told the BBC: "We are not making any such assumptions…We don't know what this drone was or why it was there." But Russia watchers are clear. "This is Russian interference," said John Lough of the New Eurasian Strategies (NEST) Centre. "It's all part of undermining support for Ukraine by pointing to the dangers of escalation and, frankly, scaring the German authorities." He sees high potential for a surge in such hybrid attacks now because Ukraine has "changed the balance" of the war. "My expectation is that such activity will increase quite sharply over the coming months. I think it's a dangerous moment." Related topics - Published2 days ago - Published1 day ago

item.title: Sudan's invisible children - born in war with no legal identity
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cr7kldz4djno?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Sudan's invisible children - born in war with no legal identity - Published Warning: This story contains details some may find distressing A 17-year-old Sudanese girl holds a young child in her arms with a heavy calm that belies her age and the concerns she has for his future. "This son of mine has no father, no birth certificate and no national number," Amira, whose name has been changed to protect her identity, tells the BBC. Looking down at him, she speaks slowly as if still trying to grasp the details of what has happened to her since the civil war erupted in Sudan. She and her family used to live in the eastern neighbourhoods of el-Fasher, a city that came under siege from the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF), which has been in a brutal power struggle with the military since April 2023. El-Fasher was the army's last stronghold in the western region of Darfur until it fell to the RSF and allied Arab militias after 18 months last October. For the tens of thousands of civilians trapped inside the city, it was a nightmare – with constant bombardment, clashes and suffering from a lack of food. In the end Amira and her family decided to flee early in 2025, desperate to find a safer area. But as they snuck out on a road south-west of the city, she says she was abducted by three armed men from the RSF and held captive. "They blindfolded me and took me to the Tabit area south of el-Fasher. I was locked in a room for two months, and every day one of them raped me in turn," she recounts in a low voice After weeks in captivity, she discovered she was pregnant and became very sick. Amira says when the men wanted to get rid of her, they dropped her near the area she had been captured. It was with the help of other people fleeing el-Fasher that she was taken to receive medical help. Months later, at a humanitarian hub that was not under RSF control, she gave birth at a hospital run by the International Medical Corps. There she received some support from a Sudanese aid organisation - the Nada Al-Azhar Foundation for Disaster Prevention and Sustainable Development (Nada). The group was also able to find her family, who had made it to a camp where hundreds of thousands of people from el-Fasher have sought refuge. It was a huge relief for them all to be reunited, but the family still face challenges - one being that eight months after giving birth, Amira has been unable to register her son's birth. "Even getting a birth notification from the hospital requires information that doesn't exist," says Amira, explaining that she is unable to provide any details about the child's father. Without this she cannot organise any official recognition of the baby's legal identity. "I can't get him vaccinated, or enrol him in nursery or school," she says. "I'm afraid for his future because he isn't registered at all. My economic situation is very difficult, and I can't afford his treatment or care. I can't even go to work for fear of being exposed to violence again." According to Nada, Amira's story is not an isolated case, but part of a reality repeated in areas experiencing conflict across Sudan. This is because many children are being born in complex circumstances, often without the knowledge of the father - meaning their births cannot be registered, explains Abu Bakr Yousif Yaqoub, Nada's director of protection programmes. "Registering a child requires identity information, a national number and a birth certificate. But when the father is absent or unknown, it becomes extremely difficult," he tells the BBC from el-Fasher. "The mother is often alone, and sometimes she herself is still a child who needs care, which limits her ability to care for her baby. "There are also health challenges related to the lack of follow-up on essential vaccinations, which begin at birth and continue through the child's early years." He warns that this situation does not just affect a child's early years but extends to their future education and as an adult being able to travel or obtain official documents. It is not easy to obtain data about the number of children that have been born as a result of rape in Sudan. According to Nada's director general, Shaza Ahmed, this comes down to social stigma as the true numbers are not recorded. "Women who experience such assaults do not feel comfortable reporting them," she tells the BBC, speaking from Port Sudan, an army-held city in the east of Sudan. "Unfortunately, most of the mothers of these children are themselves children - girls under the age of 18. Therefore, they cannot make the decision to go officially to court or the police, as they need a guardian to accompany them." She notes that 90% of the cases recorded by her organisation involve families refusing to allow official reporting of the sexual assaults that led to pregnancy. "As a Sudanese woman, my greatest fear and concern for children born as a result of rape is that we are facing a whole generation that will live under stigma, danger and fear," Ahmed says. "These children will not receive respect from society, their well-being will not be truly protected, and above all, they will not have access to services or their rights." For Ahmed they are not being treated as if they are "fully human", even though Sudanese law does grant all children the right to obtain an identity. Sudanese lawyer Majida Idris explains that the Child Act of 2010 allows for the registration of children born outside marriage. But it relies on the mother being willing to file a report that she has been assaulted - because this kick starts the registration process. Once reported, the case is then referred to social services for documentation, before being sent to the civil registry, where the child is registered under the mother's name and given a full legal name according to procedures. However, Idris says that the reality during war is completely different, especially in Darfur, where the ongoing conflict has led to the collapse of civil services and the shutdown of civil registry offices, leaving thousands of children unregistered. "The absence of documents does not just mean the absence of a piece of paper - it means denying the child access to education, healthcare and legal recognition," she tells the BBC. The lawyer says it is imperative to reactivate civil registry offices in accessible areas and intensify legal efforts to ensure children obtain their right to identity and legal recognition. Amira and her child remain in Darfur - and therefore in administrative limbo. Her mother admits that the lack of paperwork for her grandson is a worry. Yet for the moment the family is overwhelmed with gratitude to have found one another again. Amira has also been offered emotional and psychological support sessions and other advice by Nada - which is a comfort to the family. "I was so extremely worried until I found her. I hadn't been eating or drinking," Amira's mother told the BBC. "The reunion was like a miracle from God. To see our daughter back sitting among us is a gift and blessing that could not be thanked enough for."
